en: A thimble mouth, camel-calf eyes,
Great shining eyes that glanced about,
A crimson dress and a moon-slender waist—
A swaying beauty
Great Manas obtained for him.
For the companion who came without religion,
His voice when he cried out like the call to prayer,
His white turban as big as a cauldron—
Khan Manas provided a mullah.
Some of us companions came without a home.
For the companion who came without a home,
The upper edge of its lattice walls
Fastened with iron fittings,
All along the upper valance
Edged with beaver fur six fingerbreadths wide,
All its fastening bands
He had braided from pure silk;
He had a stately dwelling built to proper form—
Great Manas gave him a stately dwelling.
One companion came without livestock;
For the companion who came without livestock,
Horses with mottled heads on the foothills,
Thoroughbreds and swift steeds together,
Great Manas allotted them.
He joined what had been broken,
Gathered what had been scattered,
Kindled what had gone out,
Brought the dead to life.
Your hero Sultan Manas—
Clinging to his hem, we became men;
We became the equals of heroes' sons.
Dust rose wherever we went;
At our voices, souls departed.
Manas's salt carries a heavy debt;
Will his salt not destroy us?
Precious Manas's spirit—
Will his spirit not destroy us!
Kyrgylchal, chief of the forty,
Manas's salt is bitter;
How can we piss upon his salt?
Manas's spirit is golden;
How can we enter his camp?
As we speak, he has left behind
A noble male child;
How can we attack him?
Your khan, Manas the leopard—
While his spirit watches,
How can we attack his palace?!”
Then Kobosh blustered,
Thundering in fury:
“Always, you forty swine,
‘My lion Manas, blessed by Khydyr!’—
You shout that and leave it there!
Without even a moment's delay, forty companions,
Kyrgylchal and Tazbaimat,
You two must go at once
That wild shrew Kanykey—
Find out about the wretched woman!
If the bitch will not obey,
Drag her along the road
And have the dogs tear her apart!”
Having received his khan's command,
What could poor old Chalym do?
He slung a battle-axe at his waist
And took the familiar Tazbaimat
As his companion now.
To Khan Manas's palace
They rode and arrived.
Crying, “Oh, my gray-maned hero!”
Calling out mostly in mockery,
Whimpering, “Oh, my dear lost one!”
Swaying mostly in mockery.
Sixty women were singing laments;
Akylai sat beside the mourning effigy;
Your resolute sister-in-law Kanykey
Stood sobbing bitterly,
Wailing and crying aloud:
“Damn your fathers' graves, forty companions!
All forty of you were dogs from forty different places;
If not dogs, what sort of people were you!
When my sovereign was alive,
You went and conquered the Afghan land;
You, who would not pass without enjoying its riches—
How could Marghalan have remained unharmed?
You reached and conquered the Afghan land;
Without your wreaking havoc there,
How could Zhet-Kait have remained unharmed?
You drove white deer and made cattle of them;
You threw the places where you fought into turmoil;
You destroyed Omsk and took plunder;
When my sovereign was alive,
You broke through its midst and opened a road.
All forty of you were dogs from forty different places
When precious Manas was alive.
You became mighty cliffs blessed by Khydyr;
After my sovereign blessed by Khydyr died,
You destroyed my palace, forty companions,
And became enemies of my very self.
To plunder my fine cloth?
It was God's decree;
Are you standing here to wreak havoc today?”
Thus she sobbed and wept;
Your dear sister-in-law, for her slayer of foes,
Cried out in lament.
Casting a sidelong glance,
Kyrgylchal saw
Sixty women singing laments,
Akylai beside the mourning effigy.
He opened the curtain then
And stepped backward;
That woman Akylai—
He seized her breast then.
“To the words I say,
Will you agree, Akylai?
Kobosh sends you word:
Will you marry him, Akylai?”
“Yes, that will do, yes,” she said,
“Yes, that will be good,” she said.
“In your old age
You have come to mediate, hero,” she said.
“A woman who would not marry that son—
Seven generations of her fathers are unbelievers!”
Seeing this,
Your dear sister-in-law Kanykey
Could not contain her many troubled thoughts;
Tears streamed from her eyes in ten directions.
“Forty days had not yet passed since my sovereign died,
My sovereign, born of a falcon,
How can I let dogs born of crows
Tread upon his bed,
How can I let them bare my breast?!
My sovereign, born of a goose,
How can I let dogs born of crows
Tread upon my bed,
How can I let them open my bosom?!
I would sooner die than see this;
Rather than remain alive like this,
May I perish as though I had never been born!”
When she looked to this side—
It was sharp steel fallen from the sky,
A possession left by the generous one;
Unable to find his Zulpuqor,
She stood crying out in tears.
Your queenly sister-in-law Kanykey
Stood wailing and sobbing,
Then stood weeping and crying aloud.
Her dear quail-like eyes
Shed tears in separate streams;
Her dear currant-like eyes
Shed tears a whip's length long.
Crying out in sorrow,
Unable to find her composure,
Your precious sister-in-law cried aloud.
Her ribs seemed to split apart,
Her heart was grievously torn.
“Since my precious one died,
The full forty days have not yet passed;
Yet they stand here pressing me,
As though to take a wife and live in ease.
For gray-maned Manas, the slayer of foes,
We have not yet held the customary memorial feast.
From my head, this wretched, bereaved woman's,
The black mourning cloth has not yet been removed;
Not yet understanding spoken words,
The orphan he left behind
Has not yet begun to speak.
My forehead bone is rather curved;
When the hero died,
My prospect of making a life grew meager.
My crown hair was still all together;
When the prince died,
I had not a speck of good fortune.
It was a deep pit already dug;
What this bereaved woman had to face
Was overwhelming sorrow.
Mottled-headed horses on the foothills,
Thoroughbreds and swift steeds together—
The child to drive and tend them is young;
Brothers and close kin are all enemies.
Lulled in the lap before me,
The child my precious one left is young.
When the moon goes dark,
This is what the night is like;
When the generous one dies,
Ah, this is what a person's days are like!
Damn your fathers' graves, forty companions!
All forty of you were dogs from forty different places;
If not dogs, what sort of people were you!
Kyrgylchal, chief of the forty,
You were a wise-born hero;
Were you the one to come and mediate?!
Dragged about like the carcass in a riding game,
Was I the one to marry dogs?
When my sovereign was alive,
You crunched sugar white as snow;
You gulped spirits like water.
Entering bloodshed, you grew hardened;
All of you gathered together
And gained the name of leopard-warriors.
You became lions protected by the unseen patron;
Through my gray-maned hero you became men.
‘Marry a sightless dog,’ they say;
I am the one plunged into so much misery.
When my sovereign was alive,
You went and raided the Afghan land;
How could Marghalan have remained unharmed?
When I think of it, you are an unbeliever!
While I stand here in mourning, before my very eyes,
You lay your hand upon my breast,
Drive me to distraction,
And mock my words.
Kyrgylchal, chief of the forty,
May the written charm tied in your belt strike you!
May that oath sworn before God strike you!
How can you go about as their go-between?
How can I marry a scoundrel?
My prince, born of a falcon—
To dogs born of ravens,
How can I let my breast be bared,
How can I let my bed be trodden upon?”
Then, saying this,
Kanykey, built like a warrior,
Grew pale and stood grim,
Summoning courage, fierce and stern,
Looking like a lion,
Venom pouring from her mouth.
Her great teeth, broad as doors,
Then broke apart like millet grains;
Her thirst for blood seized her.
Kyrgylchal, who had come to mediate—
She meant to slaughter him as a sacrifice,
Drag him along the road,
And have the dogs tear him apart.
Sparing no thought for her precious life,
Your leopard sister-in-law Kanykey,
Upon the scoundrel who had come with word,
Meant to bring calamity.
That daring woman, built like a warrior,
Looked toward the women's side of the yurt:
The six sharp blades fallen from the sky
Were not hanging on the lattice wall;
No one knew where they were.
When she looked in the white chest,
For six calves and four yearling horses
The Ak-Tinte bought at that price—
Only its hilt was sticking out.
She seized it firmly by the hilt
And placed it in her right hand.
Kyrgylchal, who knew her nature,
With Tazbaimat behind him,
Made to flee with long strides.
His knees giving way in terror,
Beside Akylai,
Tazbaimat, standing between them,
When he saw Kanykey's face,
Rushed out trembling.
